Use this page if the browser primers will not run on your network, or if you
prefer to work in RStudio.

Everything taught in the browser primers is taught here, including the 2×2
table from Primer 7. The difference is that you run the code in your own R, so
you also have to load packages yourself.

::: {.callout-note}
## Run this first
Open RStudio, then run these 2 lines in the Console.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

In the browser primers these packages are loaded for you. In RStudio they are
not. Every script you write from now on starts with its `library()` lines.
:::

## Objects

`<-` puts the value on its right into the name on its left.

```r
n_screened <- 2400
district   <- "Kolar"

n_screened
district
```

Nothing prints when you assign. Typing the name on its own line prints it.

## Functions

A function takes arguments in brackets and returns a value.

```r
sqrt(144)                     # 12
round(3.14159, 2)             # 3.14
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)  # the same, with the arguments named
```

## Vectors

`c()` combines values of the same type.

```r
cases <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)

length(cases)   # 6
sum(cases)      # 124
mean(cases)     # 20.66667
range(cases)    # 11 31
```

Arithmetic applies to the whole vector at once. There is no loop to write.

```r
cases      <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)
population <- c(12000, 12000, 12500, 12500, 13000, 13000)

cases / population * 1000
```

## Types

```r
counts   <- c(14, 22, 31)                    # numeric
district <- c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan")   # character
exposed  <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)             # logical

class(counts)
```

Mixing types converts everything to the most forgiving one, usually character.
That is how a column of numbers becomes text.

## Comparison and counting

A comparison returns one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per element. `sum()` then counts, and
`mean()` gives a proportion.

```r
age <- c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45, 19, 58, 40)

age >= 45          # TRUE/FALSE for each
sum(age >= 45)     # 4
mean(age >= 45)    # 0.5
```

`mean()` of a comparison is prevalence in miniature.

## Missing values

```r
sbp <- c(128, 142, NA, 136, 151, NA, 119)

mean(sbp)                 # NA
mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)   # 135.2
sum(is.na(sbp))           # 2
```

`na.rm = TRUE` changes the question from "the mean of these 7 people" to "the
mean of the 5 we measured". Ask why the values are missing before you drop them.

## Tibbles

A tibble is several equal-length vectors side by side: one row per observation,
one column per variable.

```r
library(dplyr)

participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

participants
```

Look at any new dataset with these before you analyse it.

```r
nrow(participants)
names(participants)
str(participants)
summary(participants)
```

`$` pulls a column back out as a vector.

```r
participants$age
mean(participants$sbp)
mean(participants$smoker)          # proportion of smokers
sum(participants$sbp >= 140)       # how many have raised BP
```

`table()` counts a categorical column. It hides `NA` unless you ask.

```r
table(participants$district)
table(participants$district, useNA = "ifany")
```

## A dataset to practise on

The examples below use `survey`. Build it by running this once.

```r
library(dplyr)

set.seed(2026)

survey <- tibble(
  id           = sprintf("S%03d", 1:200),
  district     = sample(c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  residence    = sample(c("Urban", "Rural"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  sex          = sample(c("Female", "Male"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  age          = round(runif(200, 18, 80))
) |>
  mutate(
    sbp          = round(rnorm(200, 104 + 0.38 * age, 14)),
    dbp          = round(rnorm(200, 68 + 0.14 * age, 9)),
    hypertension = sbp >= 140 | dbp >= 90
  )

glimpse(survey)
```

These numbers are made up. They exist so the code below has something to run on.

## Packages

2 separate steps, and people mix them up.

| Step | Command | How often |
|---|---|---|
| Install | `install.packages("dplyr")` | once, ever |
| Load | `library(dplyr)` | every session |

`install.packages()` belongs in the Console, never in a script.

## The native pipe

`|>` puts the value on its left into the first argument of the function on its
right.

```r
# Nested: read inside out
round(sqrt(mean(c(4, 9, 16, 25, 36))), 2)

# Piped: read left to right
c(4, 9, 16, 25, 36) |>
  mean() |>
  sqrt() |>
  round(2)
```

Turn on the native pipe shortcut in **Tools → Global Options → Code → Use
native pipe operator**. The shortcut is <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>M</kbd>,
or <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>M</kbd> on macOS.

You will see `%>%` in older code. It behaves almost the same. We use `|>`
because it is part of R itself.

## The 5 dplyr verbs

| Verb | Does what |
|---|---|
| `filter()` | keeps rows matching a condition |
| `select()` | keeps columns you name |
| `mutate()` | adds or changes a column |
| `group_by()` | splits into groups |
| `summarise()` | collapses each group to one row |

```r
library(dplyr)

survey |> filter(residence == "Urban")
survey |> filter(residence == "Urban", age >= 50)
survey |> filter(district %in% c("Kolar", "Hassan"))

survey |> select(id, age, sbp)
survey |> select(-dbp)

survey |> mutate(age_group = if_else(age >= 50, "50+", "under 50"))

survey |>
  mutate(age_band = case_when(
    age < 40 ~ "under 40",
    age < 60 ~ "40-59",
    .default = "60+"
  ))
```

`filter()` drops rows where the condition is `NA`, silently. Count your rows
before and after.

```r
survey |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    mean_age     = round(mean(age), 1),
    n_hypertense = sum(hypertension),
    prevalence   = round(mean(hypertension), 3)
  )
```

Put `n()` in every `summarise()` you write. A mean over 3 people and one over
300 look the same on the page without it.

## Plots

3 pieces: the data, the `aes()` mapping, and a `geom_`.

```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(survey, aes(x = age, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point()
```

Layers join with `+`, not `|>`.

Inside `aes()` means the property comes from a column. Outside `aes()` means it
is a fixed setting for the whole layer.

```r
ggplot(survey, aes(x = age, y = sbp, colour = residence)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6)
```

```r
ggplot(survey, aes(x = sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, colour = "white")

ggplot(survey, aes(x = district, y = sbp)) +
  geom_boxplot()

ggplot(survey, aes(x = district, fill = hypertension)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

Label every plot. A title that states the finding beats one that names the
axes.

```r
ggplot(survey, aes(x = age, y = sbp, colour = residence)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title    = "Systolic blood pressure rises with age in both urban and rural adults",
    x        = "Age (years)",
    y        = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
    colour   = "Residence",
    caption  = "Simulated data for teaching."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Epidemiological measures from a 2×2

The 4 cells are called `a`, `b`, `cc` and `d`. The third is `cc` because `c()`
is a function.

<table class="twobytwo">
<tr><th></th><th>Disease</th><th>No disease</th></tr>
<tr><th>Exposed</th><td>a</td><td>b</td></tr>
<tr><th>Unexposed</th><td>cc</td><td>d</td></tr>
</table>

```r
a  <- 90
b  <- 910
cc <- 30
d  <- 970

risk_exposed   <- a / (a + b)          # 0.09
risk_unexposed <- cc / (cc + d)        # 0.03

risk_exposed / risk_unexposed          # risk ratio   3.00
risk_exposed - risk_unexposed          # risk difference 0.06
1 / abs(risk_exposed - risk_unexposed) # NNH  16.7 (harmful exposure)
(a * d) / (b * cc)                     # odds ratio  3.20
```

On the course we use `epitools`, which does this and gives confidence intervals
as well.

```r
library(epitools)

tab <- matrix(c(d, cc, b, a), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
riskratio(tab, method = "wald")
```

`epitools` wants the unexposed row first and the non-case column first. Read
the table it prints back before you trust the number.
